body_markdown:
French cars, French food, French wine… I love it all. And given how long my Simca has been sitting around, not running, and thus serving as French eye candy, you could say I’m a French sculpture connoisseur, too. I don’t speak the language, but here in our historic North Carolina ex-foundry-turned-car-commune, the Simca provides a dose of culture. We call it a *je-ne-say-hhhwhat?*


The original plan for[my 1966 Simca 1000S Bertone Coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/can-i-interest-you-in-a-foreign-investment-opportunity/) was, for the last few years… *inexistante* . My buddy Connor and I bought this thing from a Nebraska cattle ranch for something like $400. At such farm auction prices, who needs a plan?


First time seeing the light of day in a couple years.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The Simca was positioned on an elevated platform that we use for overflow parking, hanging out, cigarette smoking, or motorcycle rebuilding. As the foundry gremlins, aka car club members, moved the Simca off the platform for the umpteenth time to pressure-wash and epoxy-seal the area, I decided that it was time to put at least *some* effort into fixing the Simca.


The only microscopic bit of work I’ve done on the thing is putting a set of teeny-tiny 13-inch whitewalls on it. And that was really to facilitate shuffling it around. That even didn’t work out too well; at least one of the wheels has since rotted out around the valve stem.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


I partially rectified the situation by scouring Facebook Marketplace. for replacement tires. I took the fast and easy route, which was to buy a set of four 1970s 4×98 mm Shelby Viper (or Jellybean, Libre, whatever you want to call them)[mag wheels](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/mag-wheel-field-guide/) from an eccentric Fiat collector in Raleigh. (I can’t find any information on these wheels, so if someone knows about them, please drop knowledge in the comments!) I had my friend Adam go pick them up, and he and the seller ended up hanging out for quite a while. Turns out they knew each other. True weird-car brotherhood, right there.


Pedal-box passenger.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


This set of Jellybean mags is going to require some modification. The wheels are meant to accept a mag-style lug nut that centers on a washer and a boss on the face of the wheel. That’s not especially compatible with the BMW-style lug-bolt-mount wheels on the Simca, so we resolved to wait on this journey until the impending brake work starts. And there *will* be brake work; at present, there is a disassembled pedal box on the passenger seat.


I asked Thomas, the shop’s chief wrench, to do what I sorely wish I had time to: dig deep into the unknown to see if this poor Simca will run or not. Here is Head Gremlin’s official account:


The stool is very nearly too tall to be useful on the Simca.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


> “First, I had to start the air compressor to fill the one tire that is in rebellion and refuses to hold air. I rolled the Simca to the wash bay to give it a good pressure wash and knock off the Barn Dust.
>
>
> The pressure wash revealed that the door seals are completely toast. Of course. Next came the Comet wash, a method popularized by the great[David Freiburger](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/exclusive-whats-next-for-david-freiburger-after-roadkill/) , which revealed that the car was even more turquoise than its current Earl Scheib paint job would suggest. The paint actually came out better than I thought it would, post-Comet, and the cleanup didn’t degrade the patina one bit. If anything, the finish was more even, less rusty, and it didn’t rub off on your pant leg.
>
>
> After that, I rolled the car back inside to attempt to resurrect the engine. I noted that when the tires have air, the thing rolls like a skateboard *(I saw Thomas on CCTV walking oh-so-coolly next to the Simca as it glided out of the shop door. -Matt* )
>
>
> After sorting through the dozens of car batteries here and finding one that wasn’t completely flatlined, I established that the car was not at high risk of burning itself to the ground. It seems that the mice have left most of the wiring harness alone. Apparently, rodents aren’t as fond of French cuisine as we are, despite what a certain Disney movie might suggest.
>
>
> After confirming that I had power at least to the distributor, I sanded the points, and they seem to have come around for the most part. The cap, rotor, and contact arm appeared to be replacements for the otherwise unavailable French-imported parts. They seem to work well enough here!


Scratch, scratch… vroom.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


> On a side note, the thing has Atlas-branded spark-plug wires, which means that the person who owned this previously probably had it worked on at a Chevron full-service gas station or bought their parts from another Standard Oil-affiliated service station. Atlas parts were sold by Standard Oil in the ’50s and ’60s, and I think into the ’70s. It was essentially a store brand for the gas stations, but they were generally high-quality parts. The modern equivalent would be like going to a full-service NAPA. Side note to the side note: Atlas’ replacement headlights (in my lowly opinion) were the best sealed beams ever produced!
>
>
> Buying parts from a gas station, shockingly, didn’t seem to the reason for why the Simca was ultimately parked. So I soldiered on.


Hmmm, where does one buy a Simca speedo needle?


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


> The 944-cc inline-four engine seems to turn over fine. The starter is definitely weak and possibly dying. That’s not a huge worry as service parts are available. The low-pressure fuel pump that’s on it seems to actually be working, but I doubt the tank is any good thanks to a lost gas cap. The throttle cable is completely seized, and the linkage on the engine is completely worn out. Hand throttle it shall be.
>
>
> I tried to clean the ground cable and all of the connections leading to the engine. Although I don’t think 10 gauges of copper is good enough for this engine, even with it being as tiny as it is. It did not really seem to hit on brake cleaner, but there does seems to be some of the original 9:1 compression left. The biggest issue I fought when trying to get it to light off was the slow cranking speed and large battery draw from the starter.
>
>
> To help with that, I went through most of the ignition system to get the strongest spark possible. I confirmed that the coil is sparking very well and checked for leakage on some of the wires. At the plug, it will jump at least a 1.5-cm arc. I wire-wheeled all four plugs (because it was night and the parts house was closed) and put a little bit of gas on the intake.
>
>
> Lo and behold, it actually ran. In a furious attempt to restart it, I think I may have accidentally burned the starter up. On the bright side, it seems that we actually might have a runner… for once.”


“Am I air-cooled and, thus, valuable now?”


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


Thank you, Thomas!


As stated, the burned-up starter is not a big deal. Perhaps I’ll drop it off at Phil’s Starter & Alternator or source a replacement. If you can imagine, the Simca 1000S Bertone Coupe does have a number of cross-reference parts to the more pedestrian Simca 1000 sedan, so I’m optimistic about being able to find a new-old-stock starter or brushes, bearings, and an armature. Somewhere. Surely, it’s a worthwhile upgrade to put in a lower-resistance ground path while we’re at it.


So the Simca runs… ish. After a carb rebuild and tank flush, Thomas and I have both been motivated to start finding some brake parts to rebuild the relatively advanced four-wheel Lockheed discs and floor-mounted master-cylinder/pedal-box assembly. A Troutman Foundry vintage rally racing livery has been discussed. And I do have a set of amber Marchal rally lights to really set off the look.


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


The idea of restoring this car daunts me and seems relatively pointless considering the rich patina and seemingly low degree of expense required to get it back on the road. I suspect you’ll see me documenting a starter and brake rebuild in the next few weeks. Or maybe I’ll go deeper and eat my own words… smothered in béchamel with a glass of Provence rosé.


Apply liberally.
